subject: liston
direction_of_this_file: FROM the witness TO Melba Liston
method: One row per interview document, other than her own, in which at least one block was judged to be about her -- plus Clora Bryant, whose testimony is inside Liston's own interview. A reader saw all of a witness's blocks at once and judged the relation, the lead quote and the caption phrase. spoke_themselves=false means her name is only in the interviewer's mouth or an editor's bracket: not a witness. Quotes re-verified verbatim here; grounded=false flags a caption word the testimony never contains. A person interviewed twice (Slide Hampton) has two rows -- people.json folds them.
read_this_first: Read `caution` on every row before displaying its quote.

items.name: Randy Weston
items.context: Liston as arranger of Weston's music: Five Spot date with Coleman Hawkins (c.1959), Montreal Jazz Festival 1985 and later residency, 'Spirit of Our Ancestors', 'Khepera'
items.one_liner: relied on her arrangements, even after her stroke
items.summary: Weston said only Liston could arrange 'Spirit of Our Ancestors', told how he goaded her back to work after the stroke that left her unable to play, after which she learned to write music by computer with her left hand, and praised her genius and spiritual strength through years of illness.
items.caution: The stroke anecdote includes 'I insulted her as only musicians can do. I called her all kinds of names' and 'She cried a little bit' -- affectionate goading in context, but harsh if excerpted; avoid quoting those lines alone. Dates are Weston's recollection: he places the Hawkins Five Spot date in 1959 and the Montreal festival concert in 1985, while the interviewer dates the Montreal residency to '97 -- check against the discography. The interviewer's 'long partnership' phrase is hers, not his.
items.notes: Upstream's evidence was the interviewer's words, but the relation is amply supported by Weston's own account. Weston: 'We did, I think, three recordings after she had that stroke'. Block 309840: 'Melba did the arrangements for that' (Khepera).
items.lead_quote: Then I realized that only Melba Liston could do this.
items.second_quote: Unfortunately, she has had problems with illness. But, her spiritual strength is so powerful.

more_quotes.quote: Melba Liston did all the arrangements, by the way.
more_quotes.summary: Weston noted in passing that Liston did all the arrangements for the African night of his Montreal Jazz Festival residency.

more_quotes.quote: Melba did the arrangements for that.
more_quotes.summary: Weston mentioned that Liston did the arrangements for his 'Khepera' recording.

doc.title: Randy Weston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

relations.evidence: you and Melba Liston had such a long partnership

she_said.summary: Liston said she met Randy Weston while playing with Dizzy Gillespie at Birdland, arranged his music (including Little Niles) for some forty years with complete freedom, and credited him with pulling her through after her stroke when nobody else stuck with her.
she_said.her_quote: I’ve been writing for Randy. I’m still writing for Randy. I wrote for him up until I had the stroke. After I had the stroke and got over a little bit, I’m writing for him again. I think he pulled me out of it – helped anyway. I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.

items.name: Mary Lou Williams
items.context: Dizzy Gillespie's band at the Newport Jazz Festival; Williams's return to performing
items.one_liner: was urged by her to play again
items.summary: Williams told how Gillespie sent Liston to hear her play, how Liston reported back on her chords, and how Liston, who had taken down Williams's arrangements for Gillespie's Newport set, insisted they were Williams's own, part of the musicians' campaign to coax her back.
items.caution: Only the first name 'Melba' is used; identification with Liston rests on context (working for Gillespie, arranging for his Newport set) and is high but not explicit. Liston's quoted words are reported second-hand ('I understand') -- present them as Williams's account, not Liston's verbatim speech. The second quote is cut mid-quotation (the sentence continues 'I was in the room and I just sat down and took the music down').
items.notes: The lead line shows Liston praising Williams rather than Williams describing Liston; it is still the most vivid thing in the testimony. Block 367027: 'Dizzy called and Melba and all the musicians were trying to get me out.'
items.lead_quote: Melba, I understand, would go back and say, "Man, Lou played some chords and you ought to hear them. They're really great."
items.second_quote: She said, "I didn't do them. That was Lou's arrangement.

more_quotes.quote: Dizzy called and Melba and all the musicians were trying to get me out.
more_quotes.summary: Williams said Gillespie, Liston and other musicians were all trying to coax her back to performing.

items.name: Slide Hampton
items.context: Dizzy Gillespie big band (trombone section; Liston musical director and main arranger)
items.one_liner: learned in dizzy's band how heavy she was
items.summary: Hampton said he first met Liston in Gillespie's big band, where she sat in his trombone section and was, in substance, the musical director and main arranger, writing music 'that weighs as much as this building' beside which the men's arrangements sounded small.
items.caution: Pronoun trap in block 275470: the middle sentences ('the principal trombone player was a woman... we all aspired to the things that she could do, Janice Robinson') are about Janice Robinson in the World of Trombones; only 'Melba was the same way' onward is Liston. The quotes chosen are after that point. The claim that Hampton 'did stuff with Melba Liston' on trombone-choir records is the interviewer's (Brower), not confirmed by Hampton. 'Peep, peep, peep' could read as a slight on the band's other (male) arrangers.
items.notes: Hampton presents her explicitly as leading the band's musicians ('Over all those guys that were there, she was the musical director'), so 'played under' / liston_leads; he was also her section-mate. Upstream 'collaborated with' rested on the interviewer's words. Same person as Hamilton witness 275930; this is the stronger row. Also: 'Musically, she was heavy.' (275466).
items.lead_quote: She played really good, and she wrote music that weighs as much as this building.
items.second_quote: The men’s arrangements would sound little peep, peep, peep, around her.

more_quotes.quote: Melba Liston was the musical director. I had to go there. I had to go there and get kicked, kicked and beat-up on. I did it. They taught me a lot in there.
more_quotes.summary: Hampton recalled that Liston was musical director of Gillespie's big band when he joined, a band 'way over my head' where he was 'kicked and beat-up on' and taught a lot.

more_quotes.quote: I didn’t know that she was as heavy musically as she was. I got in that band. I learned it real fast. Musically, she was heavy.
more_quotes.summary: Hampton said he first worked with Liston in Dizzy Gillespie's band and quickly learned how musically heavy she was.

more_quotes.quote: It was Melba, and Chuck Connors, who played with Duke’s band, and another trombone player.
more_quotes.summary: Hampton named Liston in the trombone section of Gillespie's band with Chuck Connors and a 'Willie', calling them all very good players.

more_quotes.quote: Melba, being the arranger that she was, she definitely was going to write something for a trombone choir.
more_quotes.summary: In a long account of trombone choirs, Hampton remarked that Liston, 'being the arranger that she was', was certain to write for one.

relations.evidence: Melba Liston was the musical director... It was Melba, and Chuck Connors... She was the one that was the main arranger in the band... you did stuff with Melba Liston

she_said.one_liner: had him in her trombone section on record
she_said.summary: Bryant recalled that Slide Hampton was in the trombone section on one of Liston's own record dates, which Liston acknowledged as 'a different Company altogether'; after her stroke Liston said she had tried turning her trombone around to blow it like Slide Hampton, without success.
she_said.her_quote: I tried to turn the thing around and blow it like Slide Hampton, and I can’t

items.name: Clora Bryant
items.context: Smithsonian oral history interview of Liston, conducted by Bryant over two days (1996), before Liston's move back East
items.one_liner: interviewed her for the smithsonian
items.summary: Bryant, interviewing Liston, praised her arranging (the shadings, the string voicings, 'My Reverie' as one of the most beautiful things she had done), her trombone sound and her resilience after her stroke, and told her she had admired her from afar for years, had lately become bonded to her, and counted her a guiding light for many women, Bryant included.
items.caution: Bryant is the interviewer: her lines are addressed to Liston in the second person, and many are leading questions or hearsay that Liston did not confirm or corrected -- e.g. Gerald Wilson's claim that Liston recorded with Basie (Liston did not remember it), 'how you got the school systems down there' (Liston: 'I didn't get the school systems'), the Pittsburgh Jazz Orchestra/Harlem Backstreet/Pratt Institute list (Bryant says 'I'd never heard of these', i.e. read from a source), the Ellington-influence suggestion (Liston: 'I do it all from my soul'), and the State Department 'it's been said' reports. Do not present these as established facts. Bracketed passages in her blocks are transcriber summaries, not her words. 'Maybe in the last year we became bonded' means their close friendship was recent; the long admiration was 'from afar'. Second quote is about 'My Reverie' -- name the piece when displaying.
items.notes: Relation chosen as 'friend of' from her own words ('Maybe in the last year we became bonded, but I've been bonded to you a long time'; 'I know I'm dedicated'). Also supported: 'influenced by' (liston_leads) -- 'a guiding light for a lot of people, including me'; and some collaboration -- 'you did five things for me that I haven't been able to see' (pieces Liston wrote for Bryant). Other strong lines: 'Yeah. You broke the ice. You were the innovator.' (295700); 'Well, you're one in a million.' (296163); 'I liked the way you do your shadings... a lost art in arrangement' (296068); 'Randy is your horn right now' (295938).
items.lead_quote: you have been the best, Melba. You’ve been a guiding light for a lot of people, including me
items.second_quote: that is one of the most beautiful things you’ve ever done – especially the haunting sound that you get on your trombone and what you write behind what you’re doing.

more_quotes.quote: Yeah. You broke the ice. You were the innovator.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant told Liston she had broken the ice as a woman trombonist and was the innovator.

more_quotes.quote: Because you used to say, whenever you would be sad or something, you’re horn would bring you out of it, but now you can’t depend on that, so Randy is your horn right now.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant recalled Liston saying her horn used to lift her out of sadness, and said that after the stroke Randy Weston had become her horn.

more_quotes.quote: But I liked the way you do your shadings. The trumpets blare out and you drop it down and the reeds are under, and then the trumpets are – that’s – to me that’s kind of a lost art in arrangement.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant praised Liston's dynamic shadings, trumpets blaring then dropping under the reeds, as a lost art in arranging.

more_quotes.quote: And then one phrase there you really sounded like Billie Holiday.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant told Liston that one phrase of her singing on You'll Be Sorry sounded like Billie Holiday.

more_quotes.quote: You sure knew what to do. And your voicings on those strings. That’s beautiful. It’s the first time I heard you write for strings, Melba. That’s beautiful. And I’ve heard a lot of people try to write for strings, and it doesn’t have that kind of sound.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant praised Liston's string voicings on the Earth Birth Little Niles, saying others who write for strings do not get that sound.

more_quotes.quote: how much I have admired you from afar – because you really didn’t know how much until of late. Maybe in the last year we became bonded, but I’ve been bonded to you a long time
more_quotes.summary: Bryant told Liston she had long admired her from afar and had felt bonded to her well before they became close.

more_quotes.quote: your teachers thought you were a genius, and the church members too thought you were a genius, because you could do that. But it’s something that your little mind told you – which was great.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant recalled that Liston's childhood system for picking out melodies by scale number had made her teachers and church members think her a genius.

more_quotes.quote: You found that you couldn’t reach the sixth and the seventh position on it, but you overcame that by . . .
more_quotes.summary: Bryant set up the story of the child Liston being too small to reach the sixth and seventh slide positions, and Liston finished the sentence.

more_quotes.quote: Miss Hightower seemed to have had quite an attachment. She thought you were just the greatest.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant told Liston that her teacher Miss Hightower had been attached to her and thought her the greatest.

more_quotes.quote: Oh that’s where – you got stranded there.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant recalled that the band backing Billie Holiday was stranded in the South.

more_quotes.quote: Gerald said that you recorded with Basie and that the record is out now, on CD.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant passed on Gerald Wilson's statement that Liston had recorded with Count Basie and that the record was out on CD.

more_quotes.quote: You sounded good.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant told Liston she sounded good on her 1947 recording date with Dexter Gordon.

more_quotes.quote: was that the ’56 band with Dizzy, where the guys were saying, why’d you send across to the West Coast to get a you-know-what?
more_quotes.summary: Bryant recalled the 1956 Gillespie band members grumbling about Dizzy sending to the West Coast for a woman.

more_quotes.quote: Dizzy said it was because some of them had friends that they wanted to play, to take that spot, and he sent and got you.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant reported Dizzy Gillespie's account that band members wanted the chair for their friends but he sent for Liston.

more_quotes.quote: he relished telling that story, because it confirmed what he felt about – the faith that he had in you.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said Dizzy Gillespie relished telling how Liston's arrangement silenced the band, because it confirmed his faith in her.

more_quotes.quote: I heard how you got the kids to start to read music, to become interested in jazz, and how you got the school systems down there . . .
more_quotes.summary: Bryant praised what she had heard of Liston's work in Jamaica getting children reading music and interested in jazz.

more_quotes.quote: because I know that’s what we went through.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant identified with Liston's story of harassment on the road as what women musicians of their generation went through.

more_quotes.quote: That was after Dizzy’s – somebody’s band broke up and this agent said, “You don’t have to be without work. You take a girl’s group” to wherever, and that’s the way that started.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant told how an agent suggested Liston take a women's group after a band broke up, which began her all-women group.

more_quotes.quote: I know, but it was an important something.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant insisted that Liston's film work mattered after Liston dismissed it as 'just something'.

more_quotes.quote: Yeah, Major Holley. You’re always talking about him. He talked about you the whole time . . .
more_quotes.summary: Bryant recalled that bassist Major Holley, whom Liston always talked about, talked about her the whole time too.

more_quotes.quote: A lot of your arrangements, are they Ellington-inspired? I get some nuances in some of your stuff, the way you lay it out.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said she heard Ellington-like nuances in the way Liston laid out her arrangements.

more_quotes.quote: Because you probably already know before he says it, after 40 years.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant suggested that after forty years Liston knew what Randy Weston wanted before he said it.

more_quotes.quote: You’re really reaching down.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said Liston was really reaching down in writing her first piece for trombone and strings.

more_quotes.quote: That was obvious at the rehearsals for the Groove Festival. They would be waiting for you.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant recalled seeing at the Groove Festival rehearsals how many musicians were waiting for Liston to write for them.

more_quotes.quote: You helped establish the Pittsburgh Jazz Orchestra in Pennsylvania in 1964, and then you – the Harlem Backstreet Tour Orchestra.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant credited Liston with helping establish the Pittsburgh Jazz Orchestra in 1964 and the Harlem Backstreet Tour Orchestra.

more_quotes.quote: does it strike you funny, with all your experiences and your writing, technique, and expertise in doing so many – on your horn and everything – does it strike you funny or kind of sad that a large record company has never signed you to a contract?
more_quotes.summary: Bryant asked whether it struck Liston as sad that, for all her expertise, no large record company had ever signed her.

more_quotes.quote: I think I read where you said that the women were amazed that you could be up there doing what you were doing, and they weren’t allowed the freedom.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant recalled reading that women in the Middle East on the State Department tour were amazed to see Liston on the bandstand.

more_quotes.quote: that your arrangement on My Reverie – no, Anitra’s Dance – Annie’s Dance would break the ice, because there was – they recognized the theme and they liked your arrangement – treatment of it.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant reported that on the State Department tour Liston's Annie's Dance broke the ice with audiences who recognised the theme.

more_quotes.quote: you wrote a compilation of music for this tour that included excerpts from Duke and Basie and all those people.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant stated that Liston wrote the compilation of Ellington and Basie excerpts for the State Department tour.

more_quotes.quote: They had a lot of respect for you then.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said the stars Liston worked for must have had a lot of respect for her.

more_quotes.quote: Austin Cromer sings your arrangement of If You Could See Me Now. That was great.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant introduced Austin Cromer's recording of Liston's If You Could See Me Now arrangement and called it great.

more_quotes.quote: Just sometimes? This should have been one of the times.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant insisted that the If You Could See Me Now arrangement should have thrilled Liston.

more_quotes.quote: And boy, you had your wind power there. You get a long stretch without a breath there. I kept waiting for you to breathe.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant marvelled at Liston's breath control singing You'll Be Sorry.

more_quotes.quote: the fill-ins behind the phrases of the words and then behind Dizzy when he’s playing, that’s perfect. Just beautiful.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant called the fill-ins in Liston's You'll Be Sorry arrangement, behind the vocal and behind Dizzy's solo, perfect.

more_quotes.quote: That is really a beautiful arrangement on that.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant called Liston's Annie's Dance arrangement for Gillespie's band really beautiful.

more_quotes.quote: we’ve heard three different styles of your writing, because everybody refers to you as a ballad-type person, melodic and all that stuff, but you’ve thrown in the blues, and then you’ve thrown in this production.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said the recordings showed three styles of Liston's writing, against her reputation as only a ballad writer.

more_quotes.quote: When you edit it down, boy, it’s together. Whatever you take out, I don’t think it belongs in there. Whatever you leave in, it goes.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant praised how tight Liston's arrangements were after editing.

more_quotes.quote: Anybody plays like that, got to be thinking about something.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant insisted that anyone who played like Liston on My Reverie had to be thinking about something.

more_quotes.quote: And the arrangement – you set yourself up so good.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said Liston's My Reverie arrangement set up her own solo perfectly.

more_quotes.quote: Well, you’re one in a million.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant gave up pressing and told Liston she was one in a million.

more_quotes.quote: Because I want to hear you again Melba.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant told Liston she wanted to hear her play again.

more_quotes.quote: Those two or three notes, you can take them and do something magical with them.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said Liston could make something magical of the two or three notes she could still play after the stroke.

more_quotes.quote: Because that was a beautiful solo, Melba.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant praised Liston's trombone solo on a Randy Weston waltz recorded in Montreal.

more_quotes.quote: That treatment of Little Niles is very unique. It’s different and it’s good. It’s bad. It’s bad, Melba. Very good.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant called Liston's strings treatment of Little Niles unique and 'bad' in the jazz sense.

more_quotes.quote: We heard the original, and the strings, and this one, and they’re all completely different. You arranged all of them.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said the three versions of Little Niles Liston arranged were all completely different.

more_quotes.quote: the strings is really a completely huge dimension to your writing that I’d never heard before, Melba.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said the 1996 Hi-Fly showed string writing as a huge dimension of Liston's work she had never heard before.

more_quotes.quote: I heard it. I just didn’t know that was you writing it then.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant admitted she had heard Liston's 1959 Gloria Lynne string writing without knowing it was Liston's.

more_quotes.quote: You guys are so in tune to each other, you don’t need – he doesn’t have to tell you anything anyway.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said Liston and Randy Weston were so in tune that he never had to tell her anything.

more_quotes.quote: Dig deep down and write. That’s a beautiful tune, Melba.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant called Liston's song Love, I've Found You a beautiful tune.

more_quotes.quote: You just knew that you were going to be the best. You didn’t have to say it, right?
more_quotes.summary: Bryant suggested Liston had always known she would be the best without needing to say it.

more_quotes.quote: But they still won’t have it as hard as you did.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said young women musicians would not have it as hard as Liston had.

more_quotes.quote: But those schools that you helped organize and stuff like that, the kids wanted to learn, and they came there to learn, and they did learn, because you guys were teaching them.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant credited the schools Liston helped organise with children who wanted to learn and did.

more_quotes.quote: Because Melba you’ve really overcome the stroke that you had. I think you’ve made a long stride, bettering yourself to overcome that
more_quotes.summary: Bryant told Liston she had really overcome her stroke and would do even greater things back East.

more_quotes.quote: But see it’s your attitude that keeps it from being that way.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said Liston's own attitude kept people from pitying her after the stroke.

more_quotes.quote: you’ve taken it – your stroke in stride. I know a lot of people who’ve had it, and they’ve had that attitude, “Oh, woe is me.”
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said Liston had taken her stroke in stride, unlike others who fell into self-pity.

more_quotes.quote: The quality is there though, Melba.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant told Liston that though she now wrote slowly the quality was still there.

more_quotes.quote: But you did five things for me that I haven’t been able to see.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant mentioned five pieces Liston had written for her that she had not yet seen transcribed.

more_quotes.quote: They’re not going to go through what we went through to get – because there’s almost – we almost put it in their laps.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant said her and Liston's generation had almost put opportunity in the laps of today's young women.

more_quotes.quote: You have some dedicated friends back there, Melba. No jive. I know I’m dedicated, but you’ve got a whole big bunch of them out – back there.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant assured Liston that she had a big group of dedicated friends waiting in New York.

more_quotes.quote: because you’ve been such a major part of my life, really, and I’ve just – goose-bump time, your whole
more_quotes.summary: Bryant thanked the Smithsonian for letting her interview Liston, who had been a major part of her life.

more_quotes.quote: I know, but you’ve done – you’ve done it. You hear. You’ve done it to death.
more_quotes.summary: Bryant answered Liston's apology for not talking more by telling her she had done it to death.

she_said.summary: Clora Bryant conducted the interview; she said Liston had written five arrangements for her that still needed transcribing, and Liston replied that someone was already doing them.
she_said.her_quote: I watch you getting thrilled, and then I get a thrill from that.

items.name: Curtis Fuller
items.context: Quincy Jones band (with Patti Bown); also Dizzy Gillespie's band
items.one_liner: in quincy's and dizzy's bands with her
items.summary: Fuller called his relationship with Liston in Quincy Jones's band a beautiful one, said she had also been in Gillespie's band with him, and said he loved every moment he had with her.
items.caution: Fuller says 'when I first met her I didn't know Gerald Wilson was her husband' -- probably wrong: standard accounts have Wilson as the bandleader she worked for, not her husband; do not repeat it. 'I've seen her sit on the bandstand and cry' (same block as the lead) is unexplained and could read misleadingly out of context -- left out of the quotes deliberately. Transcript is garbled ('Dizzy's bandwidth me' = 'band with me'; 'had to women and it' = 'had two women in it'), and the second quote is cut from a run-on sentence that continues into his students ('Patty Bowen and I have some young kids').
items.notes: Upstream 'collaborated with' is not supported -- no joint musical work is described beyond being in the same bands. The interviewer (Brower) introduces 'that relationship'; Fuller's answers confirm it.
items.lead_quote: Oh yeah, that was a beautiful relationship.
items.second_quote: But, I love every moment that I had with Melba

more_quotes.quote: Oh, I loved every moment of it
more_quotes.summary: Fuller said he loved every moment of working with Liston and that when he first met her he did not know Gerald Wilson was her husband.

relations.evidence: Melba was also in Dizzy’s bandwidth me... I love every moment that I had with Melba... Oh yeah, that was a beautiful relationship.

items.name: Quentin "Butter" Jackson
items.qid_source: exact unique label match in wd_people
items.context: Quincy Jones band, Europe (rehearsed in Brussels); also Liston's band for Kim Weston, Atlantic City
items.one_liner: played in her band for kim weston
items.summary: Jackson recalled playing in the band Liston led for singer Kim Weston in Atlantic City, called her a great trombonist, and named her in the trombone section of Quincy Jones's European touring band.
items.caution: Archive label is 'Butter Jackson' (doc interviewee 'Quentin Jackson'); no QID in input -- do not invent one. The second quote contains an editorial insertion ('AAKE PERSSON') and a phonetic spelling ('Okie Pearson'); use the lead only, or drop the second. His praise 'Yeah, a great trombonist, too.' is in an adjacent turn, not in a block, so it is not quotable here.
items.notes: Two contexts: section-mates in Quincy Jones's band, and played under her in Atlantic City ('played under', liston_leads, would also be supported). Interviewer is Milt Hinton.
items.lead_quote: So I went to Atlantic City and played with Melba Liston. She had a band up there, for Kim Weston.
items.second_quote: the trombones, rather, was Melba Liston, Jimmy Cleveland, and we picked up AAKE PERSSON Okie Pearson, a Swedish trombone player.

more_quotes.quote: And Kim Weston, she -- so Melba had the band for Kim Weston.
more_quotes.summary: Jackson repeated that Liston had the band for Kim Weston that he went up to play in.

items.name: Benny Powell
items.context: Randy Weston's band, late 1990s (interview January 1999)
